stem: A new service expects about 1 million requests per day, spread evenly. Roughly what average request rate is that?

options.text: About 12 requests per second (1,000,000 ÷ 86,400 seconds)
options.why: A day has 86,400 seconds, so 1M/day averages about 11.6 requests per second.

options.text: About 116 requests per second (1,000,000 ÷ 8,640 seconds)
options.why: This drops a zero from the seconds in a day: there are 86,400, not 8,640.

options.text: About 694 requests per second (1,000,000 ÷ 1,440 slices of the day)
options.why: 1,440 is the number of minutes in a day, so this is requests per minute, not per second.

options.text: About 1.2 requests per second (1,000,000 ÷ 864,000)
options.why: This adds a zero to the seconds in a day and understates the rate tenfold.

explanation: Memorise 86,400 seconds per day (about 10^5). A handy rule: 1M requests/day is about 12 QPS on average, so 100M/day is about 1,200 QPS. Real traffic is not even, so you then apply a peak factor.

stem: Match each operation with its typical order-of-magnitude latency (the classic "latency numbers every programmer should know").

options.text: About 100 nanoseconds
About 0.5 milliseconds
About 10 milliseconds
About 150 milliseconds
About 1 nanosecond

prompts.text: A network round trip within the same datacenter
A random seek on a spinning hard disk
A packet round trip from California to the Netherlands and back

explanation: RAM is about 100 ns, an in-datacenter round trip about 500 µs, a disk seek about 10 ms and an intercontinental round trip about 150 ms. One nanosecond is closer to an L1 cache hit. Each step is roughly a 100× to 5,000× jump, which is why a design that adds a cross-region hop or a disk seek per request changes its whole latency budget.
reference: Jeff Dean: Latency numbers every programmer should know

stem: A social app stores 100 million new posts per day. Each post averages 500 bytes (text plus metadata, no media). Posts are kept for 5 years, and the storage layer keeps 3 replicas of everything. About how much raw storage do the posts need?

options.text: About 91 TB, from 50 GB per day over five years
options.why: This is the single-copy figure; it forgets that every byte is stored three times.

options.text: About 275 TB, which is three replicas of roughly 91 TB
options.why: 50 GB/day × 365 × 5 ≈ 91 TB for one copy, and three replicas make about 274 TB.

options.text: About 55 TB, which is one year of data kept three times over
options.why: This counts only one year (18.25 TB) and forgets the 5-year retention period.

options.text: About 2.7 PB, which is ten times the replicated five-year total
options.why: A tenfold slip, as if each post were 5 KB instead of 500 bytes.

explanation: 100M × 500 B = 50 GB/day. 50 GB × 365 ≈ 18.25 TB/year, × 5 years ≈ 91 TB, × 3 replicas ≈ 274 TB. In an interview, say the units out loud at each step; most estimation errors are a dropped factor of 10 or a forgotten multiplier such as replication or retention.

stem: An app has 10 million daily active users. Each makes about 20 API calls per day, and the busiest hour runs at 3× the daily average rate. What peak request rate should the API tier be sized for?

options.text: About 2,300 requests per second, the daily average rate
options.why: That is the average (200M ÷ 86,400). Sizing for the average means falling over every evening.

options.text: About 770 requests per second, after applying the 3× peak factor
options.why: This divides the average by 3 instead of multiplying it; the peak is higher than the average.

options.text: About 7,000 requests per second, three times the daily average
options.why: 200M calls ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 2,315 QPS on average, and × 3 ≈ 6,950 QPS at peak.

options.text: About 139,000 requests per second, from 200M ÷ 1,440
options.why: Dividing by 1,440 gives calls per minute, not per second; the units were mixed up.

explanation: Total calls = 10M × 20 = 200M/day. Average = 200M ÷ 86,400 ≈ 2,315 QPS. Peak = 3 × 2,315 ≈ 6,950 QPS. You then add headroom (for example, size so peak runs at 60-70% of capacity) and allow for losing a zone.

stem: A service handles a steady 2,000 requests per second, and each request spends an average of 250 ms inside the service. On average, how many requests are in flight inside the service at any moment? Type just the number.
explanation: Little's Law: L = λ × W = 2,000 req/s × 0.25 s = 500 requests in flight. It holds for any stable system regardless of the arrival distribution, so it is the quickest way to size thread pools, connection pools and worker counts. If latency doubles at the same arrival rate, concurrency doubles too, which is why a slow dependency can exhaust a pool that was fine yesterday.

stem: A live-streaming event has 1 million concurrent viewers, each pulling an average of 5 Mbps. Edge servers have 100 Gbps of network capacity, and the team runs them at no more than 80% utilisation. Ignoring redundancy, what is the minimum number of edge servers?

options.text: 50 servers: 5 Tbps of egress divided by 100 Gbps per server
options.why: Right total, but it runs every NIC at 100%, ignoring the stated 80% ceiling.

options.text: 63 servers: 5 Tbps of egress divided by 80 usable Gbps each
options.why: 1M × 5 Mbps = 5,000 Gbps, and 5,000 ÷ 80 = 62.5, which rounds up to 63.

options.text: 500 servers: 40 Tbps of egress divided by 80 usable Gbps each
options.why: This treats 5 Mbps (megabits) as 5 MB/s (megabytes), inflating the egress eightfold.

options.text: 1 server: one million viewers at 5 Mbps is only about 5 Gbps
options.why: 1,000,000 × 5 Mbps is 5,000,000 Mbps, which is 5 Tbps, not 5 Gbps: three orders of magnitude off.

explanation: Egress = 1,000,000 × 5 Mbps = 5,000,000 Mbps = 5,000 Gbps = 5 Tbps. Usable per server = 100 × 0.8 = 80 Gbps. 5,000 ÷ 80 = 62.5, so 63 servers before any N+1 or zone redundancy. Bandwidth is quoted in bits (Mbps, Gbps) while storage is in bytes; mixing them is an 8× error.

stem: A read-heavy catalog has 50 million items of about 2 KB each. Reads are skewed: the hottest 20% of items receive 80% of reads, and the skew is stable. The team plans a cache in front of the database. Which statements are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: The hot 20% of items is about 20 GB of raw value data, before per-key and allocator overhead
options.why: 50M × 20% = 10M items, and 10M × 2 KB = 20 GB.

options.text: A cache that holds the hot 20% should reach roughly an 80% hit ratio at steady state
options.why: If the hot set fits and the skew holds, those 80% of reads are served from cache.

options.text: A cache node with exactly 20 GB of memory is enough, because key and allocator overhead are negligible
options.why: Keys, metadata, fragmentation and eviction headroom all need memory; size well above the raw data.

options.text: The full data set is about 1 TB, so caching all of it is out of reach for a modest cluster
options.why: 50M × 2 KB = 100 GB, not 1 TB. Caching everything is plausible here.

options.text: The database must handle about 20% of reads normally, and close to 100% briefly after a cold cache restart
options.why: Misses fall through to the database, and an empty cache sends everything there until it warms.

options.text: At an 80% hit ratio, average read latency falls to about 80% of the database's latency
options.why: The average is 0.8 × cache latency + 0.2 × database latency, which is much closer to 20% of database latency.

explanation: Hot set = 10M × 2 KB = 20 GB; full set = 100 GB. A cache holding the hot set captures about 80% of reads, leaving the database about 20% in steady state. But the database must also survive a cold start (or a cache node failure), when the miss rate jumps toward 100%. Average latency is a weighted mean: with a 1 ms cache and 10 ms database, 0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 10 = 2.8 ms.

stem: A request must pass through three services in series, each 99.9% available. It also needs one of two redundant replicas of a fourth component, each 99% available, where either replica is enough. Assume failures are independent. Which is closest to the expected unavailability over a 30-day month?

options.text: About 4 minutes, since the redundant pair lifts the whole path to 99.99%
options.why: Redundancy only helps the fourth component; the three serial 99.9% services still dominate.

options.text: About 43 minutes, since the weakest serial link sets 99.9% overall
options.why: Serial availabilities multiply, so three 99.9% links are worse than any single one.

options.text: About 2.2 hours, since overall availability works out near 99.69%
options.why: 0.999³ ≈ 0.99700, the pair gives 1 − 0.01² = 0.9999, and the product is ≈ 0.99690.

options.text: About 9.3 hours, since the 99% component caps the path near 98.7%
options.why: This treats the pair as a single 99% component and ignores the redundancy.

explanation: Serial components multiply: 0.999³ ≈ 0.997003. Parallel components multiply their unavailabilities: 1 − 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.9999. Overall = 0.997003 × 0.9999 ≈ 0.996903, so about 0.31% unavailable. 0.0031 × 720 h ≈ 2.2 hours. In practice, replicas often fail together (shared deploys, configs or zones), so real redundancy is worth less than the independence math suggests.
reference: Google SRE book: Embracing Risk; Availability table

stem: A search request fans out to 100 leaf servers in parallel and must wait for all of them. Each leaf is usually fast, but 1 in 100 of its responses takes 1 second or more, independently of the others. What fraction of user requests take at least 1 second?

options.text: About 1%: the parallel calls overlap, so the request inherits the 1% tail of a single leaf
options.why: Parallelism hides the average, not the tail. The request waits for the slowest of 100 calls.

options.text: About 63%: the chance that at least one of the 100 leaves is slow is 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰
options.why: 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.366, so about 63% of requests hit at least one slow leaf.

options.text: Essentially 100%: with 100 leaves at a 1% tail, one slow leaf is expected in every single request
options.why: One slow leaf is expected on average, but by chance 37% of requests still see none.

options.text: About 10%: tail probabilities grow roughly with the square root of the fan-out width
options.why: There is no square-root rule here; independent events combine as 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ.

explanation: P(no slow leaf) = 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.366, so P(at least one) ≈ 63.4%. This is the core result of Dean and Barroso's "The Tail at Scale": at high fan-out, a leaf's rare p99 becomes the common case for the user. That is why large systems manage leaf tail latency directly, with hedged requests, micro-partitioning and good-enough partial results.
reference: Dean & Barroso, The Tail at Scale (CACM 2013)

stem: A search root fans each query out to 100 leaf servers and waits for all of them, so rare slow leaves dominate its tail latency. To cut that tail, the team adds hedged requests. If a leaf has not answered within the 95th-percentile latency for that request type, the root sends the same request to another replica and uses whichever answer arrives first. About how much extra leaf load does this add, and why does it work?

options.text: About 100% extra load, because every request is sent twice, but each pair finishes at the faster of two latencies
options.why: That describes sending both copies up front. Waiting until p95 means only the slow 5% are duplicated.

options.text: About 5% extra load, and it works because the second replica rejects the duplicate request as soon as the first one finishes
options.why: Right load, wrong mechanism. The gain comes from a second, independent chance of a fast answer, not from deduplication.

options.text: About 5% extra load, because only requests slower than p95 are re-sent, and a replica's slowness is usually transient and uncorrelated
options.why: Only about 5% of requests pass p95 and get a second copy, which usually lands on a replica that isn't stalled.

options.text: About 50% extra load, because hedges pile up in the queues of slow replicas and are retried again
options.why: A hedge is sent once and goes to a different replica; it does not chain retries.

explanation: Deferring the hedge until p95 bounds the extra load to about 5% of requests, as "The Tail at Scale" reports. It works because most tail latency is transient (GC pauses, queueing, background compaction) and not shared across replicas, so the second copy is usually fast. Hedging does not help when slowness is correlated, such as an overloaded shared dependency. There it adds load to the thing that is already struggling.
reference: Dean & Barroso, The Tail at Scale (CACM 2013)

stem: Which statement best describes horizontal scaling compared with vertical scaling?

options.text: Horizontal scaling moves a server to a bigger machine with more CPU and RAM, with no code changes
options.why: That is vertical scaling (scaling up). It has a hard ceiling and leaves a single point of failure.

options.text: Horizontal scaling adds more machines and spreads work across them, which needs state managed outside each node
options.why: Scaling out adds capacity and fault tolerance, but work must be divisible and state shared or partitioned.

options.text: Horizontal scaling splits one application into microservices, each owned by a separate team
options.why: That is an organisational and architectural decomposition, not a scaling dimension in itself.

options.text: Horizontal scaling adds read replicas only, while all writes must stay on a single, larger primary node
options.why: Read replicas are one form of scaling out, but horizontal scaling is not limited to databases or reads.

explanation: Vertical scaling (bigger box) is simple but limited by the largest available machine, and that machine stays a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (more boxes) is open-ended, but needs a way to route work (load balancing, partitioning) and to handle shared state.

stem: A web tier that keeps user sessions in an external store (such as Redis) or in signed cookies can add and remove instances behind a load balancer without sticky sessions.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: if no instance holds per-user state, any instance can serve any request.

options.text: False
options.why: Sticky sessions are only needed when state lives in an instance's memory; here it does not.

explanation: Making the request-handling tier stateless is the standard first step to scaling it out. Instances become interchangeable, so autoscaling, rolling deploys and crash recovery stop logging users out. The state still exists; it has moved to a store designed to be shared and replicated.

stem: Which statements are true of a layer-7 (HTTP-aware) load balancer compared with a layer-4 (TCP) one? (Choose two.)

options.text: It can route requests by URL path, host or header, such as sending `/api/*` to one pool and `/static/*` to another
options.why: It parses HTTP, so routing can use anything in the request.

options.text: It can spread individual HTTP/2 requests from one client connection across several backends
options.why: It terminates the client connection, so it balances per request rather than per TCP connection.

options.text: It is always faster than a layer-4 balancer, because understanding the protocol lets it skip work
options.why: Parsing HTTP and terminating TLS costs more CPU per request; layer-4 forwarding is cheaper.

options.text: It cannot carry WebSocket traffic, so real-time apps must sit behind a layer-4 balancer instead
options.why: Common layer-7 balancers (NGINX, Envoy, AWS ALB) proxy WebSocket upgrades.

options.text: It forwards packets without terminating TLS, so it never needs access to the certificates
options.why: That describes layer-4 TLS passthrough. A layer-7 balancer must decrypt to see the HTTP request.

explanation: A layer-4 balancer picks a backend per TCP connection and forwards bytes, which is fast but blind to HTTP. A layer-7 balancer terminates the connection (and usually TLS), so it can route by content, retry idempotent requests and balance each multiplexed HTTP/2 or gRPC request. With layer 4, one long-lived gRPC connection pins all of a client's calls to one backend.

stem: A report API sits behind a load balancer using round robin across 10 identical servers. Most requests take 20 ms, but about 1 in 50 runs an export that takes 5 seconds. Some servers are often swamped while others are idle. Which balancing policy fits best?

options.text: Weighted round robin, giving each server a weight equal to its number of CPU cores
options.why: The servers are identical, so the weights are equal and nothing changes. The cost of each request is still ignored.

options.text: Source-IP hashing, so that each client always lands on the same server and warms its caches
options.why: Hashing ignores current load. A heavy client concentrates its exports on one server.

options.text: Least outstanding requests, which sends each new request to the server with the fewest in flight
options.why: A server stuck on slow exports has more in flight, so new requests go elsewhere.

options.text: Uniform random choice, which evens out the load across all ten identical servers over a long enough period
options.why: Random gives the same expected balance as round robin and still ignores in-flight work.

explanation: Round robin and random assume every request costs the same. When costs vary by orders of magnitude, a load-aware policy (least connections or least outstanding requests) routes around servers that are busy right now. Moving long exports to an async job queue would be better still.
reference: Google SRE book: Load Balancing in the Datacenter

stem: An instance is being removed from a load-balanced pool during a scale-in. Put the steps in the order that avoids dropping any in-flight requests.

options.text: Deregister the instance from the load balancer's target group, which starts connection draining
The load balancer stops sending new requests to the instance
In-flight requests finish, or the deregistration delay runs out
Stop the application process and terminate the instance

explanation: Draining (AWS calls it the deregistration delay) separates "no new work" from "kill the process". Terminating first, or stopping the process before the balancer has stopped routing, turns every scale-in and deploy into a burst of 502s. Set the delay a little longer than your slowest legitimate request.
reference: AWS Elastic Load Balancing: Deregistration delay

stem: A cache cluster has 10 nodes. Clients pick a node with `hash(key) % N`. The team adds an 11th node. Roughly what fraction of keys now map to a different node, and how would consistent hashing compare?

options.text: About 9% move with modulo hashing, and about 9% with consistent hashing too
options.why: Only consistent hashing limits moves to the new node's share. Modulo reshuffles nearly everything.

options.text: About 91% move with modulo hashing, but only about 9% with consistent hashing
options.why: A key stays put only if h mod 10 = h mod 11, which is true for 1 in 11 keys.

options.text: About 50% move with modulo hashing, and about 9% with consistent hashing
options.why: Modulo is much worse than half; only 10 of every 110 hash values keep their node.

options.text: About 91% move with modulo hashing, and none with consistent hashing using virtual nodes
options.why: The new node must take ownership of some keys, about 1/11 of them. Virtual nodes even out that share; they don't remove it.

explanation: With modulo hashing, a key keeps its node only when h mod 10 equals h mod 11. Over any run of 110 hash values that happens 10 times, so 1/11 ≈ 9% stay and about 91% move, which looks like a near-total cache flush. Consistent hashing moves only the keys the new node takes over, about 1/(N+1) ≈ 9%. Virtual nodes spread that share evenly across the existing nodes.
reference: Karger et al., Consistent Hashing and Random Trees (1997)

stem: An app keeps login sessions in each instance's memory and relies on cookie-based sticky sessions. Users get logged out whenever the autoscaler removes an instance or a deploy rolls through, and a few instances run much hotter than the rest. Which changes fix the root cause? (Choose two.)

options.text: Move session data to a shared, replicated store such as Redis, and look it up by session ID
options.why: Instances become interchangeable, so losing one loses no sessions and stickiness is no longer needed.

options.text: Replace server-side sessions with signed, expiring tokens that carry the session claims
options.why: The state travels with the client and any instance can verify it, so no server holds it.

options.text: Switch affinity from cookies to source-IP hashing so that users stay on one instance more reliably
options.why: The state still dies with the instance, and clients behind a shared NAT skew load even more.

options.text: Raise the connection-draining timeout to an hour so that sessions can finish before an instance stops
options.why: This slows scale-in and deploys, and it does nothing for crashes. The state is still trapped on one node.

options.text: Run more, smaller instances so that each failure logs out a smaller share of users
options.why: This shrinks each incident but keeps the cause. Every removal still logs people out.

explanation: The root cause is per-instance state. Either externalise it (a shared session store) or make it client-held (signed tokens such as JWTs, ideally short-lived with a revocation strategy). Both make the tier stateless, which also fixes the uneven load: once stickiness goes, the balancer can spread requests freely.

stem: An API tier autoscales at 70% CPU. Each instance has a 50-connection database pool. During a traffic spike, p99 latency goes from 80 ms to 4 s, but instance CPU stays near 25%, so nothing scales. The database shows 100% of its connection slots in use and long lock waits. What is the best reading of this?

options.text: The CPU target is too high; lowering it to about 20% would trigger the scale-out this spike needs, adding instances until latency recovers
options.why: More instances bring more pools: N × 50 connections pile more load onto the database that is already the bottleneck.

options.text: The bottleneck is the database, not the API tier; fix it there, and scale the API on concurrency or latency instead of CPU
options.why: Threads are blocked waiting on the database, so CPU is the wrong saturation signal.

options.text: The instances are too small; moving them to larger types would add the capacity the spike needs
options.why: Bigger API boxes add CPU the tier isn't using. The wait is in the database.

options.text: Autoscaling is reacting too slowly; a shorter cooldown would let new instances join faster
options.why: Nothing triggered at all, and new instances would only add database connections.

explanation: An I/O-bound tier blocks on a downstream dependency while its CPU looks idle. Scaling it out multiplies connections and makes database contention worse. Fix the constraint (slow queries, locks, pool sizing, read replicas, caching), and give the tier a saturation signal that reflects its real limit, such as in-flight requests or queue depth, plus load shedding when the dependency is saturated.
reference: Google SRE book: Handling Overload; Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: Twenty independent load-balancer nodes each pick a backend by "least outstanding requests", using their own local counts. Request costs vary widely. When a fresh backend joins the pool, every balancer sees it at zero, sends it a burst at the same moment, and its latency spikes. Which change best fixes this without a central coordinator?

options.text: Have all 20 balancers keep shared load counters in Redis and read them on every routing decision
options.why: This adds a synchronous network hop and a central bottleneck to every request, and the counts are still stale under bursts.

options.text: Pick two backends at random and send the request to the less loaded one (power of two choices), with a slow-start ramp
options.why: Random sampling stops all balancers converging on the same "best" backend, and slow start eases new ones in.

options.text: Switch every balancer to plain round robin, so that no backend is ever chosen more often than another
options.why: This removes the herd but brings back the imbalance from variable request costs.

options.text: Increase the health-check frequency so that each balancer sees the new backend's load sooner
options.why: Health checks report up or down, not load. Each balancer still acts only on its own counts.

explanation: Greedy least-load on stale or partial information causes herding: everyone picks the same minimum. The power-of-two-choices result (Mitzenmacher) shows that comparing just two random candidates gives almost all the benefit of full least-load, and it is robust to stale data because different balancers sample different pairs. Pair it with slow start (NGINX `slow_start`, Envoy slow-start mode) for new or recovering hosts.
reference: Mitzenmacher, The Power of Two Choices in Randomized Load Balancing

stem: A load test of a clustered service gives these results: 4 nodes → 4,000 req/s, 8 → 6,500, 16 → 7,200, 32 → 6,000. Each node broadcasts cache invalidations to every other node, and writes take a cluster-wide lock. Which conclusions are justified? (Choose two.)

options.text: Throughput falling as nodes are added points to a coherency cost that grows faster than linearly with node count
options.why: All-to-all invalidation is O(N²) chatter, the coherency term in the Universal Scalability Law.

options.text: Amdahl's law alone cannot explain the data, because contention by itself only flattens throughput toward a ceiling
options.why: A serial fraction caps the speedup but never makes more nodes slower. A drop needs a crosstalk term.

options.text: The serial fraction is about 50%, which by Amdahl's law is what makes 32 nodes slower than 16
options.why: Under Amdahl, any serial fraction still gives throughput that rises (or holds) with more nodes; it can't decline.

options.text: Adding still more nodes will recover throughput once the caches on the new nodes are warm
options.why: Coherency cost grows with every node added, so more nodes push throughput down further.

options.text: The load generator must be the bottleneck, since a saturated client would make results drop
options.why: A saturated client produces a flat ceiling, not lower throughput as the cluster grows.

explanation: Gunther's Universal Scalability Law models throughput as N / (1 + σ(N − 1) + κN(N − 1)). The σ term (contention, like Amdahl) causes a plateau; the κ term (coherency, such as nodes keeping each other in sync) causes retrograde throughput past a peak. The fix is to cut cross-node coordination: partition ownership so that invalidations are targeted, and replace the global lock with per-key or per-shard locking.
